newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to cooperate with major nations on forex - MOF.
newsitem.headline: Japan to cooperate with major nations on forex - MOF.

text.p: Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said on Monday that Tokyo would keep cooperating with major nations to help stabilise foreign exchange markets.

"We would like to continue to work towards stabilising foreign exchange markets through cooperation with major nations in economic policy and in the currency market," Mitsuzuka said in a speech to the Lower House of the parliament.
He also said that the government would keep careful watch over stock market movements.
"Various interest rates remain at low levels, helped by steps taken to ease monetary policy. We would like to watch over the impact of that (on the economy)," Mitsuzuka said.

Mitsuzuka said that Japan's economy is continuing to recover at a gradual pace. Private sector demand is increasing in firmness and some improvement can be seen in employment conditions, although the situation remains severe, he said.
The government intends to continue managing the economy appropriately to strengthen the recovery and put the economy on a stable growth trend in the medium to longer term, he said.

Despite severe fiscal conditions, the government gave priority to basic research in its state budget for the fiscal year starting in April, which will help the structural reforms to the economy, he said.
Mitsuzuka also said Japan would work to pass the budget for next fiscal year quickly, along with a supplementary budget for 1996/97, so there would be no gaps in government spending.
He said the global economy as a whole was continuing to grow, with stable economic expansion in the United States and gradual improvements seen in European economies.
Mitsuzuka said a planned consumption tax hike to five percent from the current three percent in April would be implemented to make up for previous tax cuts.
The measure would also help revitalise the economy in the medium- to long-term by providing funds to cope with a rapidly ageing population.
Mitsuzuka also said that Japan would make efforts to change its tax system to cope with changes such as rapid internationalisation.

Mitsuzuka stressed the importance of fiscal consolidation and said Tokyo would work to achieve its aim of reducing the fiscal deficit to three percent of gross domestic product before a self-imposed deadline of fiscal 2005/06. The cabinet had also decided to cap growth in central government spending to below the rate of nominal economic growth, he said.

The minister said Japan would set up a meeting of senior government and party officials to draw up bills for fiscal consolidation and there would be an early review of planned government spending for the 1998/99 budget.

Mitsuzuka said that although Japan's planned "Big Bang" reforms were needed to make way for the efficient use of the country's personal savings of about 1,200 trillion yen, they would also bring about risks and pain for market participants.

He said the government would take the necessary steps to speed up disclosure and clarify rules for gauging the health of banks. It would also take special care to stabilise Japan's financial system and to establish a supervisory system which could cope with the internationalisation of banking operations.
